topicName: Mixed Precision Training (FP16, BF16, FP8) and Numerical Stability

[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Mixed Precision Training (FP16, BF16, FP8) and Numerical Stability"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Deep learning models have grown exponentially in parameter size, requiring massive computational resources and memory bandwidth. Mixed precision training has become an essential technique to accelerate training throughput and reduce memory footprint without sacrificing model accuracy."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding Floating-Point Formats"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Standard training historically relied on FP32 (Single Precision). Modern accelerators introduce alternative formats: FP16 (Half Precision), BF16 (Brain Floating Point), and FP8 (8-bit Floating Point). Each format balances dynamic range and precision differently."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"FP32: 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, 23 mantissa bits. Standard precision with large dynamic range, but high memory cost."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"FP16: 1 sign bit, 5 exponent bits, 10 mantissa bits. High precision for gradients, but narrow dynamic range leading to underflow and overflow issues."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"BF16: 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, 7 mantissa bits. Shares the same dynamic range as FP32, making it robust against numerical underflow without requiring loss scaling."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"FP8: 1 sign bit, with varying exponent and mantissa configurations (e.g., E4M3 or E5M2). Maximizes hardware throughput on modern architectures like NVIDIA Hopper."},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"Numerical Stability Challenges in FP16"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Because FP16 has a narrow dynamic range (minimum positive value roughly 6.1e-5), gradients computed during backpropagation frequently underflow to zero. To prevent this, gradient scaling is required."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"scaler = torch.cuda.amp.GradScaler()
for inputs, targets in dataloader:
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    with torch.cuda.amp.autocast():
        outputs = model(inputs)
        loss = loss_fn(outputs, targets)
    scaler.scale(loss).backward()
    scaler.step(optimizer)
    scaler.update()"},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"Implementing Mixed Precision with PyTorch"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"PyTorch provides native tools via torch.amp to handle mixed precision training automatically. Operations like matrix multiplications and convolutions run in FP16 or BF16, while sensitive operations like reductions and normalization layers remain in FP32."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"import torch

model = MyLargeModel().cuda()
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-4)

# Using bfloat16 avoids explicit gradient scaling
with torch.autocast(device_type="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
    inputs = torch.randn(8, 3, 224, 224).cuda()
    outputs = model(inputs)
    print(outputs.dtype)"},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices for Stable Training"},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Always keep master weights in FP32 format while performing forward and backward passes in reduced precision."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use BF16 instead of FP16 when hardware supports it (Ampere architecture or newer) to avoid tuning GradScaler parameters."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Monitor loss spikes and inf/nan values in gradients when experimenting with FP8 or custom quantization schemes."}]
